St. Paisius Velichkovsky

Saints

St. Paisius Velichkovsky

St. Paisios Velichkovsky · St. Paisie of Neamț · St. Peter Velichkovsky

Period
1722–1794
Region
Poltava;Kyiv;Wallachia;Mount Athos;Moldavia
Titles / vocation
Monastic · Abbot · Writer · Translator
Commemoration
November 15

Introduction

St. Paisius is remembered for monastic leadership and translation of the Fathers. His life moved between Ukrainian, Romanian and Athonite settings before his final years at Neamț.

Background

Born Peter at Poltava in 1722, he was one of twelve children of a priest’s family. He studied at the Moghila Academy, then sought monastic formation and an experienced elder. His early rassophore name was Platon.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Early family,education and search

McGuckin distinguishes Paisius’s unfinished autobiography from later lives by disciples. His survey identifies the short account by Vitalis, the Slavonic biography by Metrophanes, and Gregory’s 1817 printed life. It also describes the later Platon compilation, published in Romanian in 1836 and Slavonic at Optina in 1847. These layers explain why later biographies are not all independent contemporary witnesses. The essay identifies Paisius’s native Poltava and the Romanian setting of much of his mature work.

[2] Illumined in the Spirit,Collected Studiesvol3,SVS Press,2017,pp263–280;authorized web presentation,not a free reproduction licence · Life and Early Formation:biographical sources

Life and notable events

After years in Romanian sketes and on Athos, his growing brotherhood eventually settled at Dragomirna. War, refugees, plague and political changes disrupted the community. It moved to Secu and then, in 1779, to the larger Neamț monastery. The OCA places his final fifteen years there, translating patristic writings.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Athonite formation and Moldavian communities

McGuckin locates the importance of Paisius in the renewal of the Philokalic tradition: patristic study, spiritual eldership and prayer of the heart. He follows the influence of disciples and later readers in Russia and Ukraine, including the Optina elders, St. Ignatius Brianchaninov and St. Theophan the Recluse. The essay’s interpretation of this transmission belongs to its named Orthodox scholar; it does not make Paisius a resident elder at Optina or turn a historical description into a personal prayer rule for this reader.

[2] Illumined in the Spirit,Collected Studiesvol3,SVS Press,2017,pp263–280;authorized web presentation,not a free reproduction licence · Concluding discussion of the school and reception

The survey describes his collaboration with Romanian monks Macarius and Hilarion in patristic Greek. Rather than treating inherited Slavonic manuscripts as sufficient, his translation work involved searching Greek exemplars and comparing texts. The essay connects that work with both Athos and Dragomirna.

[2] Illumined in the Spirit,Collected Studiesvol3,SVS Press,2017,pp263–280;authorized web presentation,not a free reproduction licence · Priest and Translator:language and manuscripts

At Neamț the OCA recounts an expanding brotherhood and the introduction of an Athonite Typikon. Archbishop Ambrose’s 1790 visit is associated with his elevation to archimandrite.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Neamț and1790 visit

Death and martyrdom

The OCA dates his repose to November 15, 1794, after four days of illness. He had ceased new translation work and was reviewing earlier translations. After a final farewell and Communion, he died in his cell; no execution or martyrdom is described.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Closing illness and repose

Writings and legacy

Metropolitan Tikhon’s 2025 letter calls Paisius a transmitter of Byzantine hesychastic tradition among Slavic and Romanian peoples. The letter uses his November 15 commemoration at the beginning of the Nativity Fast to discuss prayer, study and service. It is a contemporary primatial application of his legacy, distinct from either a documentary biography or an app-created devotional direction.

[3] Primatial letter,November15,2025 · Opening paragraphs and application
